code.title: Parse a raw HTTP request into its parts

followUps: A path parameter says which thing you want, and a query parameter says how you want the list or the result shaped. In GET /api/v1/orders/5 the 5 is a path parameter: without it the URL points at a different resource. In GET /api/v1/orders?status=shipped&page=2 the parts after ? are query parameters: they filter, sort or page, and they are optional. A simple test: if leaving the value out should give a 404, it belongs in the path; if leaving it out should give a sensible default, it belongs in the query string.

On the request you nearly always see Host (which site), Authorization (who is calling, usually Bearer <token>), Accept (the format wanted back), Content-Type and Content-Length (when there is a body) and User-Agent. On the response you see Content-Type, Content-Length, Date and Cache-Control. In a system with tracing you also see traceparent, the W3C header that carries the trace id from service to service so one request can be followed through the logs.

Because the HTTP standard gives a body on GET no defined meaning, so anything between the client and the server is free to ignore or drop it. A cache builds its key from the method and the URL only, so two GETs with different bodies would get the same cached answer. Some proxies and gateways strip the body or reject the request, and the browser fetch function refuses to send a GET with a body at all. Put small inputs in the query string, and for a large filter use POST /orders/search with the filter in the body.

Because when the server remembers nothing between calls, any server can answer any request. You can put 2 or 20 identical copies behind a load balancer, add more when traffic grows, and remove or restart one without logging anybody out. With in-memory sessions, user Ann's second request must reach the same server as her first (sticky sessions), or the session must be copied between servers, and a crash loses every session on that machine. Stateless servers avoid all three problems. The state still exists; it lives in the token the client sends and in the database.

It travels with every request, normally as a signed token in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header. The token (a JWT) holds claims such as the user id, roles and an expiry time, and it is signed by the identity provider, for example Microsoft Entra ID. Each server checks the signature, issuer, audience and expiry, then reads the user from the claims, with no lookup in shared memory. The other common choice is a cookie holding an encrypted ticket or a session id that is looked up in a shared store such as Redis; the server process itself still holds nothing.

HATEOAS (hypermedia as the engine of application state) means each response includes links that tell the client what it can do next, so the client follows links instead of building URLs. An order that can still be cancelled would carry a link such as "cancel": "/api/v1/orders/5/cancel"; once it has shipped, the link is simply absent. An honest answer for most teams: yes, in a limited form. Paging responses with a next link, the Location header on 201 and 202, and status links for long-running jobs are all hypermedia. Full link-driven clients are rare, because a front end built by the same team usually hard-codes its routes.

code.title: Idempotent PUT and DELETE versus POST on retry

followUps: Yes: the client sends a unique Idempotency-Key header and the server remembers the key together with the response it gave. If the same key arrives again, the server returns the saved response and does not repeat the work. Example: a payment POST with key 6f1a… charges the card and returns 201; the reply is lost, the client retries with the same key, and gets the same 201 with no second charge. Store the key in the same database transaction as the business change, and put a unique constraint on it so two simultaneous copies cannot both run.

A PATCH that describes a change relative to the current value is not idempotent. With JSON Patch, this body appends a new item every time it is sent:

[{ "op": "add", "path": "/items/-", "value": { "sku": "M-7" } }]

Send it twice and the order has 2 extra mugs. "Increase quantity by 1" is the same kind of problem: 2, then 3, then 4. By contrast a merge patch such as { "status": "shipped" } sets an absolute value, so sending it twice leaves the same state. That is why PATCH is listed as "not guaranteed idempotent": it depends on the body.

Things you never asked for will change your data, because the whole web assumes GET is harmless. Browsers prefetch links, search crawlers follow them, email security scanners open every link in a message, and proxies or client libraries retry a GET that timed out. If GET /orders/5/delete exists, any of those can delete the order. The reverse also hurts: a cache may answer the GET itself, so the change you wanted never reaches the server. It is also an easy attack, since a hidden <img src="…/delete"> on another site makes the victim's browser send the GET with their cookies.

code.title: Choosing 401, 403 or 404

followUps: You return 404 on purpose when even the existence of the thing is private. If user Bob asks for /orders/5 and it belongs to Ann, a 403 tells him "order 5 exists, you just cannot see it", and by trying ids 1 to 10,000 he can map which ones exist. A 404 gives him the same answer as for an id that was never used, so he learns nothing. GitHub does this for private repositories. Use 403 when existence is not a secret, for example a normal user calling /admin/reports. Whichever you choose, apply it the same way on every endpoint.

All three mean "the server side failed", but they point at different places. 502 Bad Gateway: a proxy or gateway reached the server behind it and got a broken answer, for example the app crashed or closed the connection. 503 Service Unavailable: the server cannot take the request right now, because it is overloaded, starting up or in maintenance; it often carries Retry-After. 504 Gateway Timeout: the proxy waited for the server behind it and got no answer in time. In practice: 502, look at whether the app is running; 503, look at load and health checks; 504, look for a slow query or a timeout set too low on the gateway.

307 and 308 keep the method and the body; 301, 302 and 303 may not.

CodeLastsMethod on the new request
301permanentclients may change POST to GET
302temporaryclients may change POST to GET
303temporaryalways GET (used after a form POST)
307temporarysame method and body
308permanentsame method and body

So when an API moves and clients POST to it, redirect with 308, or the POST may silently become a GET.

Use POST /api/v1/orders/search with the filter in the JSON body. A query string has practical length limits (many servers and proxies stop at a few thousand characters), it is written to access logs, and nested conditions are awkward to encode. The search POST returns 200 with the results, not 201, because nothing was created. The price is that the result is not cacheable by URL. If caching or sharing a result matters, create the search as a resource instead: POST /searches returns 201 with an id, and GET /searches/{id}/results?page=2 is then a normal cacheable GET.

I make /orders?customerId=42 the main route, because an order is a top-level thing that people also filter by status, date and product, and one collection with filters covers all of those. I use nesting when the child cannot exist without its parent, such as /orders/5/items, and I keep it to one level deep. Offering /customers/42/orders as well is fine as a shortcut, as long as both run the same query and the same permission check. What I avoid is long chains like /customers/42/orders/5/items/3, which are hard to route and force the client to know the whole path.

I return 200 OK with the updated order, so the client sees the new status without a second call:

POST /api/v1/orders/5/cancel
200 OK
{ "id": 5, "status": "Cancelled", "cancelledAt": "2026-01-10T09:00:00Z" }

Other outcomes: 409 Conflict with a problem-details body if the order has already shipped, 404 if it does not exist or is not the caller's, and 202 Accepted with a status URL if cancelling takes time (for example a refund through a payment provider). Cancelling an order that is already cancelled returns 200 again, so a retry is harmless.

code.title: PUT replaces, PATCH merges

followUps: Yes, when the client chooses the URL of the new thing. PUT /users/42/settings/theme or uploading a file with PUT /files/report.pdf means "make this URL hold this content": the first call creates it and returns 201 Created, later calls replace it and return 200 or 204. This stays idempotent, because sending it twice leaves the same single resource. Use POST when the server picks the id. If you want "create only, never overwrite", the client adds If-None-Match: * and the server answers 412 when the resource already exists.

You send the field with the value null; in JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) null means "remove this field".

PATCH /api/v1/orders/5
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json

{ "note": null, "status": "shipped" }

This clears note, sets status, and leaves every other field alone. Two limits follow from that rule: you cannot store a real null as different from "missing", and you cannot change one element of an array, because an array in the patch replaces the whole array. If you need either, use JSON Patch (RFC 6902) with explicit operations.

You apply the patch to a copy of the data and then validate the result, because the patch alone cannot tell you whether the final object is valid.

  1. Load the entity and map it to an update DTO.
  2. Apply the patch to the DTO, never straight to the EF Core entity (that would allow over-posting).
  3. Validate the DTO, and return 400 with the errors if it fails.
  4. Map the DTO back and save.
var dto = mapper.ToUpdateDto(order);
patch.ApplyTo(dto, ModelState);          // JsonPatchDocument<UpdateOrderDto>
if (!TryValidateModel(dto)) return ValidationProblem(ModelState);
mapper.Apply(dto, order);
await db.SaveChangesAsync();

It pays off where the allowed actions depend on the state of the data. If an order response contains a cancel link only while cancelling is allowed, the front end shows the button when the link is there and does not copy the business rule ("not shipped, not older than 30 days"). When the rule changes, only the server changes. The other everyday wins are paging (next links let the server switch from offset to cursor paging without breaking anyone) and long-running jobs, where the 202 response links to the status URL. For a plain CRUD API with one front end, the extra work rarely pays for itself.

No. The model measures how much an API uses the ideas of REST, not how good it is. gRPC, GraphQL and JSON-RPC all send everything to one endpoint by design and are good tools: gRPC gives a strict contract and speed, GraphQL lets the client choose fields. Level 0 is a problem when an API is sold as REST over HTTP but ignores HTTP: every call is a POST that returns 200 with "success": false in the body. Then caches, retries, monitoring by status code and standard tools all stop working, and each client has to learn your private rules.

Paging links are the most common real use of level 3: the response tells the client the URL of the next page, so the client follows it instead of calculating it.

{ "items": [ ... ],
  "links": { "next": "/api/v1/orders?cursor=eyJpZCI6ODB9", "prev": null } }

Some APIs put the same information in a Link header with rel="next". The benefit is freedom to change: the server can move from ?page=3 to a cursor, or change the page size, and clients that only follow next keep working. When next is missing, the client knows it has reached the end.

code.title: Offset paging repeats rows, keyset paging does not

followUps:
You add a unique column, normally the id, as a tiebreaker, so the sort order is total and the cursor holds both values. If 3 orders share the same CreatedAt and the page ends on the second of them, "after this date" alone would skip or repeat the third.

SELECT TOP (50) Id, CreatedAt, Total FROM Orders
WHERE CreatedAt < @lastDate
   OR (CreatedAt = @lastDate AND Id < @lastId)
ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC;

The cursor returned to the client is the pair (CreatedAt, Id) of the last row, encoded so clients treat it as opaque. A composite index on (CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC) lets the database seek straight to the position, in O(log n + page size).

Return the items plus enough for the client to ask for the next page without doing any maths:

{ "items": [ ... 50 orders ... ],
  "nextCursor": "eyJkIjoiMjAyNi0wMS0xMCIsImlkIjo4MH0",
  "hasMore": true }

For offset paging, return page, pageSize and, if it is cheap enough, totalCount. Many APIs return ready-made next and prev links instead of a bare cursor. I leave the total out by default on large tables, because counting all matching rows can cost more than fetching the page; a hasMore flag (fetch 51 rows, return 50) is nearly free.

Because the database cannot jump to row 1,000,000; it has to read and throw away every row before it. OFFSET 1000000 ROWS FETCH NEXT 50 ROWS ONLY produces 1,000,050 rows in sorted order and discards the first million, so the cost grows with the page number: page 1 is instant, page 20,000 takes seconds. Keyset paging replaces the skip with a WHERE on the sort key, which an index can seek to directly, so every page costs about the same: O(log n + page size) instead of O(offset + page size). Deep offset pages also drift when rows are inserted, as the program above shows.

A breaking change is anything that can make a client that works today fail without the client changing. Typical ones: removing or renaming a field or endpoint; changing a field's type or format (number to string, a different date format); making an optional request field required; tightening validation; changing a status code or the error shape; changing default behaviour such as sort order or page size. Safe changes are additions: a new optional request field, a new response field, a new endpoint. One trap: a new enum value in a response is technically an addition but breaks clients that switch on a fixed list, so tell clients up front to tolerate unknown values.

Two: the current version and the one before it, with a published date for when the older one is switched off. For a public API I would give at least 6 to 12 months of overlap; for an internal API with a few known teams, a quarter is often enough. Every live version has a cost: its own tests in the pipeline, security fixes applied twice, and a mapping layer each time the data model changes. Three or more versions usually means deprecation dates were never enforced. I measure calls per version and per client, so the decision to remove one is based on numbers.

You declare that the controller serves both versions and map only the changed action to the new one, so everything else is shared. With the Asp.Versioning package:

[ApiVersion("1.0")] [ApiVersion("2.0")]
[Route("api/v{version:apiVersion}/orders")]
public class OrdersController : ControllerBase {
    [HttpGet("{id}")] public Task<OrderV1Dto> Get(int id) { ... }          // v1 and v2
    [HttpGet("{id}"), MapToApiVersion("2.0")] public Task<OrderV2Dto> GetV2(int id) { ... }
}

In a real controller you also mark the old action with MapToApiVersion("1.0") so the two routes do not clash. Both actions call the same service; only the DTO mapping differs, so business logic is not copied.

code.title: Exceptions mapped to Problem Details responses

followUps:
You register one exception handler that recognises the exception type and writes a problem-details response with status 409. Since .NET 8 the clean way is IExceptionHandler:

public class ConflictHandler(IProblemDetailsService problems) : IExceptionHandler {
  public async ValueTask<bool> TryHandleAsync(HttpContext ctx, Exception ex, CancellationToken ct) {
    if (ex is not ConflictException) return false;          // let the next handler try
    ctx.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status409Conflict;
    return await problems.TryWriteAsync(new() { HttpContext = ctx,
      ProblemDetails = { Title = "Conflict", Detail = ex.Message, Status = 409 } });
  } }

Wire it with AddProblemDetails(), AddExceptionHandler<ConflictHandler>() and app.UseExceptionHandler(). Controllers then just throw, and no action needs a try/catch.

It comes from the distributed trace that ASP.NET Core starts for every request. When a request arrives, the framework creates an Activity; if the caller sent a W3C traceparent header, the same trace id is continued, otherwise a new one is made. The id is available as Activity.Current?.Id, with HttpContext.TraceIdentifier as the fallback, and the built-in problem-details writer adds it to the response as traceId. Because logs and Application Insights record the same id, a support engineer can paste the value from a user's error message and find every log line and downstream call for that request.

Mostly no: the server should send a stable machine-readable code and the client should choose the words. Give each error a fixed identifier (the type URI, or an extra field such as "code": "ORDER_ALREADY_SHIPPED") plus a default English title and detail for developers and logs. The front end maps the code to text in the user's language, which keeps wording and tone in one place and lets it change without an API release. If the server must produce user-facing text, for example validation messages, pick the language from the Accept-Language header. Either way, never make clients parse the message text to decide what happened.

code.title: ETag and a conditional GET returning 304

followUps: no-cache means "you may keep a copy, but ask the server before every use"; no-store means "never keep a copy at all". With no-cache the browser stores the response and sends a conditional request each time (If-None-Match); if nothing changed it gets a small 304 and reuses its copy, so you save bandwidth and still always show current data. With no-store nothing may be written to the browser cache or any proxy, so every request downloads the full body. Use no-store for sensitive data such as bank statements or personal details, and no-cache for data that must be fresh but is not secret.

You either tell the CDN to drop the entry or you change the URL so the old entry is never asked for again. Three tools, used together:

  • Purge: when the data changes, call the CDN's purge API for that URL or for a tag that groups related URLs.
  • Versioned URLs for static files: app.3f9a1c.js with a one-year max-age; a new build has a new name, so nothing needs purging.
  • Short lifetimes for API data: s-maxage=30 with stale-while-revalidate, so the worst case is 30 seconds stale and no purge is needed.

Purging is not instant across all edge locations, so do not rely on it for data that must be exact.

HTTP caching stores the response outside your server (browser, CDN, proxy), so a repeat request may never reach you; output caching stores the response inside your server, so the request arrives but the endpoint code is skipped. The practical difference is control. With HTTP caching you hand out a lifetime in Cache-Control and cannot take a copy back from a browser. With ASP.NET Core output caching (AddOutputCache, CacheOutput()) the server decides the key and can evict at once, for example by tag when an order changes. They combine well: output caching protects the database, HTTP caching saves the network trip.

code.title: Which requests need a CORS preflight

followUps: Requests the browser calls "simple" go out without a preflight. That means the method is GET, HEAD or POST, the only headers set by script are the safe-listed ones (Accept, Accept-Language, Content-Language, Content-Type), and Content-Type is one of text/plain, multipart/form-data or application/x-www-form-urlencoded. So a plain GET for public data skips it, but almost every real API call does not: sending JSON (application/json), adding an Authorization header, or using PUT, PATCH or DELETE each triggers the OPTIONS preflight. Same-origin calls involve no CORS at all.

Let the browser cache the preflight answer, or remove the need for CORS altogether.

  • Send Access-Control-Max-Age: 7200 on the preflight response. The browser then reuses the answer for that URL and method instead of asking again. Browsers cap the value (Chromium-based ones at 2 hours).
  • Serve the API from the same origin as the page, for example by routing /api through the same host with a reverse proxy. Same origin means no preflight ever.
  • Avoid extra custom headers, since each new header name can force a fresh preflight.

In ASP.NET Core the first one is policy.SetPreflightMaxAge(TimeSpan.FromHours(2)).

Because CORS is enforced only by browsers, and Postman is not a browser. The server answered both calls; the browser then refused to hand the response to your JavaScript because the CORS headers were missing or wrong. The usual causes: the page's origin is not in the allowed list (check scheme and port: http://localhost:4200 is not https://localhost:4200); the OPTIONS preflight gets 401 or 405 because authentication runs before CORS (call UseCors before UseAuthentication); or cookies are sent while the server answers with the wildcard origin *, which browsers reject. Read the console message and look at the OPTIONS request in the network tab.

code.title: Token bucket rate limiter returning 429

followUps: Rate limiting refuses requests above a limit; throttling slows them down or makes them wait. With a rate limit of 100 requests a minute, request 101 gets 429 Too Many Requests at once. With throttling, request 101 is queued or delayed and answered later, so the caller sees a slower response, not an error. In .NET's rate limiter the difference is one setting: QueueLimit = 0 rejects, QueueLimit = 20 lets 20 requests wait for a free slot. People often use the two words for the same thing, so in an interview say which behaviour you mean.

It should stop sending, wait for as long as the server says, and then try again a limited number of times.

  1. Read the Retry-After header (seconds or a date) and wait at least that long.
  2. If the header is missing, back off exponentially with some random jitter: about 1 s, 2 s, 4 s.
  3. Give up after 3 to 5 attempts and report the failure.
  4. Fix the cause: batch calls, cache results, or reduce parallel requests.
if (res.status === 429) {
  const wait = Number(res.headers.get("Retry-After") ?? 2 ** attempt);
  await sleep(wait * 1000 + Math.random() * 250);
}

Retrying immediately only uses up the next window and keeps you blocked.

Limit by cost instead of by request count: give each caller a budget of points and let each endpoint spend a different number. With a token bucket of 100 tokens a minute, a simple GET takes 1 token and a report export takes 50, so a caller can make 100 reads or 2 exports. .NET's limiter supports this through the permit count in AcquireAsync(permitCount). Two simpler options often suffice: a separate, stricter policy on the expensive endpoint, or a concurrency limit ("at most 2 exports running per client"). For very heavy work, move it to a background job so the limit applies to jobs queued.

code.title: CRUD actions and their status codes

followUps: Because the entity is the shape of your database, and the response is a promise to your clients, and those two must be free to change separately. Returning the entity leaks columns clients should not see (password hash, internal flags, cost price), and renaming a column becomes a breaking API change. Navigation properties cause trouble too: the serializer can follow Order.Customer.Orders into a cycle or trigger lazy loading, which means one extra query per row. On input the same shortcut lets a caller set any column (over-posting). A small DTO per endpoint, filled with a Select projection, also makes the SQL fetch only the columns needed.

In three layers, each catching a different kind of mistake.

  • Shape, at the edge: required fields, ranges and formats on the request DTO, with data annotations or FluentValidation. [ApiController] returns a 400 problem-details response automatically before the action runs.
  • Business rules, in the service or domain: "an order that shipped cannot be cancelled", "stock must be available". These need data, and return 409 or 422.
  • Database constraints, as the last line: unique indexes, foreign keys and not-null columns catch what two simultaneous requests can slip past the code.

The controller itself should hold none of these rules.

In the query that loads the order, using the user id from the token, never an id sent by the client. [Authorize] on the controller only proves the caller is logged in; it knows nothing about order 5.

var userId = User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier);
var order = await db.Orders
    .Where(o => o.Id == id && o.CustomerId == userId)
    .Select(o => new OrderDto(o.Id, o.Total))
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync(ct);
return order is null ? NotFound() : Ok(order);

Putting the owner in the WHERE means a missed check cannot return someone else's row. For richer rules (owner or support staff) use resource-based authorization: IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(User, order, "CanView").

code.title: Route group with endpoint filters, modelled with delegates

followUps: Choose controllers when you need their built-in features or your team already knows them: heavy use of filters, model binding with complex rules, OData, or an existing large controller code base you are not going to rewrite. Minimal APIs are lighter and start faster, and are my default for new services with fairly small surfaces. Both use the same routing, authentication and middleware, so mixing them in one app is fine. The choice is mostly about how you want to organise 80 endpoints, not about capability.

An endpoint filter wraps one endpoint (or a route group) and sees the typed arguments, while middleware wraps every request and sees only the HttpContext. A filter can read the bound DTO, validate it and return Results.ValidationProblem(...) before the handler runs; middleware cannot do that, because binding has not happened yet. Use middleware for things that apply to the whole app (logging, exception handling, CORS) and filters for per-endpoint concerns such as validation or idempotency keys.

Move each feature's endpoints into its own static class with an extension method, and call them from Program.cs:

public static class OrderEndpoints {
  public static IEndpointRouteBuilder MapOrders(this IEndpointRouteBuilder app) {
    var g = app.MapGroup("/api/v1/orders").RequireAuthorization();
    g.MapGet("/{id}", GetOrder); g.MapPost("/", CreateOrder);
    return app;
  } }
// Program.cs: app.MapOrders(); app.MapCustomers();
Handlers are plain static methods that take their services as parameters. Program.cs then stays about 30 lines, and each feature lives in one folder.

I prefer code-first for a team that owns both the API and its clients and wants speed: write controllers, generate the document, and check it in a pull request. I prefer contract-first when several teams or outside partners build against the API at the same time, because they can agree on the document first and generate server stubs and client SDKs in parallel. The risk of code-first is accidental breaking changes, so I diff the generated document in CI. The risk of contract-first is the document and code drifting apart, so I run contract tests against it.

Since .NET 9 the template has built-in AddOpenApi() and MapOpenApi(), which serve the JSON document at /openapi/v1.json but include no UI. To show a page, add a UI package that reads that document: Swashbuckle.AspNetCore.SwaggerUI, Scalar.AspNetCore or NSwag. For example app.MapScalarApiReference() in the development environment only. Many teams keep the UI off in production and publish the JSON document to an API portal or API Management instead.

Declare a security scheme in the document, then say which operations use it. For a bearer token the scheme is type: http, scheme: bearer, bearerFormat: JWT, and for Entra ID sign-in it is type: oauth2 with the authorization-code flow, the authorization and token URLs, and scopes (use placeholders, not real tenant ids). Then add a security requirement on the operations that need it. In .NET 9 and later you add this with a document transformer. The UI then shows an Authorize button, and generated clients know to send the header.

code.title: Content negotiation from the Accept header

followUps: Accept is sent by the client and says which format it wants back; Content-Type says which format the body in this message is in. A request that sends JSON and wants CSV has Content-Type: application/json and Accept: text/csv. A response also carries Content-Type, which is the format the server actually chose. If the server cannot produce any acceptable format it should return 406 Not Acceptable; if it cannot read the request body's format, it returns 415 Unsupported Media Type.

Register an output formatter for CSV and let content negotiation choose. In ASP.NET Core, write a class that inherits TextOutputFormatter, add text/csv to its supported media types, and add it with options.OutputFormatters.Add(...) and ReturnHttpNotAcceptable = true. The action returns Ok(list) as usual. A client that sends Accept: text/csv gets rows, one that sends application/json gets JSON. A cheaper alternative is a separate route such as /orders.csv, which is easier to open from a browser link.

Vary tells caches which request headers changed the response, so they do not serve the wrong version. If /orders returns JSON for one client and CSV for another, and the CDN stores the first answer under the URL alone, the next client gets the wrong format. With Vary: Accept the CDN keeps one copy per distinct Accept value. The cost is a lower hit rate, so vary only on headers that really change the body (Accept, Accept-Encoding, sometimes Accept-Language), never on User-Agent or Cookie.

code.title: Optimistic concurrency with ETag and If-Match

followUps: Use a pessimistic lock when conflicts are frequent and a lost update is expensive, so retrying is worse than waiting. Examples: seat booking where two people click the same seat at once, or decrementing stock on a hot item. Then the database holds a lock (SELECT ... WITH (UPDLOCK)) for the short time of one transaction. Do not hold a lock across HTTP requests, because a user who opens an edit form and leaves would block everyone. Optimistic concurrency works best for forms where conflicts are rare, like editing a profile.

A strong ETag means the bytes are identical; a weak ETag (written W/"v7") means the content is equivalent in meaning but may differ in bytes. Strong tags are required for safe range requests and for If-Match on updates in the HTTP rules, because "equivalent" is not good enough to prove nothing changed. Weak tags suit cache validation, for example when gzip or a timestamp changes the bytes but not the data. In practice a database rowversion turned into a quoted string is a fine strong ETag.

Apply the same rule: the client sends the ETag of the whole resource it read, even if it changes one field, and the server compares it against the current version. It does not matter that the patch is small, because another user may have changed a different field and the combined result could break a business rule. If you accept that, you can instead merge non-overlapping field changes, but that is a deliberate design choice. Return 412 on a mismatch and 428 when If-Match is missing, so the client reloads and retries.

code.title: Idempotency key makes a POST safe to retry

followUps: Store them in a table (or Redis) with a unique constraint on the key, and let the database settle the race. Two identical requests in the same millisecond both try to insert the key; one succeeds and the other fails with a duplicate error. The loser then either waits and returns the saved response, or answers 409 Conflict with a hint to retry. Save the key in the same transaction as the business change, so there is never a payment without a key or a key without a payment. Keep keys for about 24 hours, then delete them.

The client generates it, usually a GUID per user action. Only the client knows which attempts are retries of the same intention. If the server made the key, a retry after a lost response would not carry one, and the server could not tell it from a new action. The client must reuse the same key for every retry of one action and make a fresh key for the next action. Keep the key with the pending action (for example in the form state), not generated inside the retry loop.

A unique constraint on the business data (for example one payment per order id) blocks real duplicates, but it cannot return the first call's original response and it does not cover cases where the data legitimately repeats. A customer may buy 2 identical coffees in 2 separate orders; nothing in the data separates a retry from a second order. The idempotency key carries the client's intention, so the server can tell "same attempt again" from "a new purchase". Use both: the key for retries, the constraint as a safety net.

code.title: 202 Accepted and a status endpoint for a long job

followUps: The server tells it, or the client backs off. Put Retry-After: 5 on the 202 and on every status reply, so the server controls the poll rate and can raise it when it is busy. If there is no hint, the client starts at 1 to 2 seconds and doubles up to a ceiling of about 30 seconds, adding a little random jitter so many clients do not poll in step. Polling a status row is cheap, but 10,000 clients polling every second is not, so for many clients use a webhook or push (SignalR) to notify on completion instead.

The job must be safe to restart, or it is lost half done. Put the work on a durable queue (Service Bus, a database table) where a message is only removed after success; if the worker dies, the message becomes visible again and another worker picks it up. That means the work must be idempotent: for an import, use upserts keyed by the row id, or record a checkpoint ("rows up to 40,000 done") so a rerun skips finished rows. After a set number of failed attempts the message goes to a dead-letter queue and the job status becomes Failed with a reason.

Stream the response when the result is produced gradually and the client can use it as it arrives, and the whole thing fits in one connection's lifetime, for example exporting 50,000 rows as a CSV download with IAsyncEnumerable, or a chat answer streamed as server-sent events. Use a job when the work may take minutes or hours, must survive a closed browser tab or a server restart, or the result is wanted later or by someone else. Rule of thumb: if the client has to stay connected to see progress, stream; if it can leave and come back, use a job.

code.title: Retry with backoff and a circuit breaker

followUps: Because the first request may have succeeded even though you never saw the answer. A timeout does not mean "it did not happen". If you retry POST /payments, the card may be charged twice. Retries are safe for GET, PUT and DELETE, which are idempotent. For POST, retry only when the call carries an Idempotency-Key and the other side honours it, or when the error proves the request never ran (connection refused, before any byte was sent). Polly's default retry handler in AddStandardResilienceHandler does not retry POST for this reason.

A retry storm is when a service slows down, every client retries, and the extra traffic keeps the service down. If 1,000 clients each retry 3 times, the struggling service receives up to 4,000 calls. Prevent it with: exponential backoff plus jitter so retries spread out; a small retry limit (2 or 3); a retry budget (retry at most 10% of calls); a circuit breaker to stop calls for a while; and retrying at only one layer, since three layers that each retry 3 times turn one call into 27.

Closed, open and half-open. Closed: calls pass through and failures are counted. When failures reach a threshold (for example 50% of the last 20 calls, or 5 in a row), the breaker moves to open: calls fail at once, with no request sent, for a break period such as 30 seconds. After that it goes half-open: it lets one or a few trial calls through. If they succeed it returns to closed; if one fails it goes back to open. This gives the failing service room to recover and gives callers a fast error instead of a long wait.

code.title: BOLA owner check and mass assignment DTO

followUps: BOLA example: GET /api/v1/invoices/1043. The user is logged in, and by changing the number to 1044 they receive another customer's invoice, because the code only checked that a token exists. The fix is to include the owner in the query: db.Invoices.Where(i => i.Id == id && i.CustomerId == userId) where userId comes from the token claim, and return 404 when nothing matches. Add an integration test that logs in as user A and requests user B's id. Random GUID ids make guessing harder, but they are not a fix.

Mass assignment (over-posting) is when the API binds the request body straight onto an entity, so a caller can set fields they should not. If Order has IsPaid and CustomerId, a body with "isPaid": true may mark it paid. Fix: bind to a DTO that contains only the allowed fields (as the program above does), or use an explicit allow-list when mapping. Never accept an entity as the action parameter, and keep sensitive fields such as role or price out of any input type.

You cannot protect what you do not know about, so build an inventory. Sources: the gateway's request logs (every path actually called), the generated OpenAPI document compared with the real route table, and a scan of old versions, /v1 paths, test and debug endpoints that were never removed. Anything called but not documented, or documented but unowned, gets an owner or gets deleted. Put the inventory in the API portal, require every route to appear in the OpenAPI document in CI, and put a retirement date on every old version.

First understand why, and offer something concrete. Ask what blocks them (a release freeze, vendor code, budget) and give a firm last date in writing. Options: extend that one client by a fixed period with a signed end date; offer a compatibility layer, where the gateway translates old requests to the new API for them only; or help with the migration by providing a client SDK, a test sandbox and engineers' time. An extension is a business decision, so involve the account owner. Never extend without an end date, because the next client will ask for the same.

Design for change from the start so breaking changes are rare. Add fields, never remove or repurpose them; make new request fields optional with defaults; tell clients to ignore unknown response fields; use opaque cursors and ids so you can change internals; return enums as strings clients can tolerate if extended; and use contract tests in CI to detect an accidental break. Collect a list of "things we wish we had changed" and batch them into one planned major version, not one per quarter.

More than people expect: every extra version means another set of tests in the pipeline, security patches applied to 2 branches, a mapping layer between old DTOs and the new data model, documentation and support to maintain, and developers who must remember the old behaviour. A rough guide is that each live major version adds 10 to 20 percent to the cost of changing the API. That is the argument I use when a stakeholder wants to keep v1 "just in case": show the real call count and the engineering cost, and agree a date.

A WSDL (Web Services Description Language) file is the XML contract of a SOAP service. It lists the types (XML Schema for the messages), the messages, the port type (the operations and which message goes in and out), the binding (SOAP version and style) and the service with its endpoint address. Tools read it to generate client code, so a client can call GetCustomer(42) as a normal method. It is the SOAP equivalent of an OpenAPI document, but it is the primary way SOAP clients are built.

WS-Security protects the message, and HTTPS protects the connection. With HTTPS the data is encrypted only between two hops; if a message passes through an intermediary, such as a broker or a gateway that terminates TLS, it is readable there. WS-Security can sign and encrypt parts of the XML message itself, so it stays protected end to end, and it carries tokens (SAML, username tokens, X.509). That is why banks and government systems still use it. Today most new APIs rely on HTTPS plus OAuth 2.0 tokens, which is simpler.

SOAP reports errors with a Fault element inside the response body, usually with HTTP status 500. The fault has a Code (such as Sender or Receiver, saying who is at fault), a human-readable Reason, and an optional Detail with application-specific data, which a WSDL can describe as typed fault contracts. This differs from REST, where the HTTP status code carries the main meaning. A client library turns a Fault into an exception, for example a FaultException in WCF.

A binding says how a WCF service talks: the transport (HTTP, TCP, named pipes, MSMQ), the message encoding (text XML, binary, MTOM) and the security and reliability settings. basicHttpBinding is plain SOAP 1.1 over HTTP, wsHttpBinding adds WS-Security and transactions, and netTcpBinding is fast binary over TCP between .NET programs. The service contract stays the same; only the binding in configuration changes. This was powerful but hard to configure, and the many knobs were a common source of production problems.

CoreWCF supports the common server scenarios: SOAP over HTTP and TCP, basicHttpBinding, wsHttpBinding, netTcpBinding, and WS-Security with transport and message security for many cases. It does not cover everything: named pipes and MSMQ support is limited, WS-AtomicTransaction and some WS-* features are missing or partial, and so are some federation and reliable messaging scenarios. Always check the supported-features list against the bindings your existing service really uses before promising a migration date.

Because gRPC fits the way most WCF services were used internally: a typed contract (.proto instead of an interface and WSDL), fast binary messages, streaming, deadlines and code generation for many languages, all on HTTP/2 and fully supported in modern .NET. It is also far simpler than the WS-* stack. For services that had to remain SOAP for partners, the advice was CoreWCF. The answer is "use the right tool": gRPC for internal service-to-service calls, REST or CoreWCF for outside callers, and do not pick gRPC only because it is newer.

Run the old and new endpoints side by side and compare their answers. Record real requests (or take them from logs), send each to both services, and diff the responses, field by field, ignoring fields that differ by design such as timestamps. This is called shadow traffic or a parallel run. Add contract tests from the WSDL, and a few golden-file tests for tricky operations. Start with read-only operations, where a difference harms no one, then move writes, where you need a small share of live traffic (canary) and a quick rollback switch.

WS-AtomicTransaction lets a transaction span several services, and neither CoreWCF nor the modern stack supports it well. Do not try to recreate it. Replace distributed transactions with a design that tolerates failure: one local transaction per service, plus a saga or compensating actions ("if payment fails, release the stock") and an outbox for reliable messages. That is a real design change, so find these operations in the inventory early and estimate them separately, since they are usually the riskiest part of the project.

Frame it as risk and cost, not as technology. The old runtime (.NET Framework and WCF) gets no new features, needs Windows servers and licences, and is hard to hire for. The benefits to name: lower hosting cost (Linux containers), faster releases, security patches, and the ability to scale. Show a plan with small steps, each of which delivers something and can be rolled back, plus a date when the old system is switched off and its cost disappears. Promise that customers see no change, and measure it with the parallel-run results.

code.title: Protobuf varint encoding versus JSON size

followUps: Protobuf sends numbers, not names, and packs them tightly. JSON repeats every field name as text in every message ("productId":150), writes numbers as digits, and adds quotes, colons and braces. Protobuf sends a one-byte tag for the field number and a compact variable-length number, so productId=150, quantity=2 is 5 bytes against 30 as JSON, as the program above shows. The saving is smaller for long strings. The cost is that the bytes are unreadable without the .proto file, so you cannot just look at a message in a browser.

gRPC errors are a status code plus a message, not HTTP statuses. The codes include NOT_FOUND, INVALID_ARGUMENT, PERMISSION_DENIED, UNAUTHENTICATED, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED and UNAVAILABLE. On the server you throw new RpcException(new Status(StatusCode.NotFound, "Product 7 not found")), and the client catches RpcException and reads StatusCode. For richer detail use the Google rich error model (google.rpc.Status with typed details) sent in trailers. Retry only for UNAVAILABLE and similar transient codes.

gRPC uses long-lived HTTP/2 connections, so a plain layer-4 load balancer connects a client to one server and keeps all its calls there, even if 1 client sends 90% of the traffic. Fixes: use a layer-7 proxy that understands HTTP/2 and balances each call (Envoy, YARP, Azure Application Gateway, or a service mesh); or use client-side balancing, where the client knows all server addresses (DNS or Kubernetes headless service) and rotates calls; or set a maximum connection age on the server so clients reconnect regularly. In Kubernetes the default service does not balance gRPC well.

code.title: gRPC style deadline and server streaming

followUps: The framework cancels the call: it fires the CancellationToken in ServerCallContext.CancellationToken, and the client receives DEADLINE_EXCEEDED. If the handler passes that token to its database and HTTP calls, they stop early. If it ignores the token, the work keeps running and is wasted. In .NET the deadline also travels to the next service in the chain through the grpc-timeout header, so a chain of calls shares one overall budget. Always give calls a deadline; the default is none, which means waiting forever.

Authentication is added as call credentials: a bearer token in the request metadata. On the client, use CallCredentials or an AsyncAuthInterceptor that adds Authorization: Bearer <token>, and always use TLS so the token is protected. On the server, ASP.NET Core authentication middleware validates the JWT as for any API, and you add [Authorize] to the gRPC service class. Mutual TLS (client certificates) is the other common option for service-to-service calls inside a trusted network.

An interceptor is gRPC's middleware: code that wraps each call on the client or server, so cross-cutting work lives in one place. Typical uses: logging, adding the auth token or a correlation id to the metadata, mapping exceptions to status codes, metrics, and retries. In .NET you inherit Interceptor and override a method such as UnaryServerHandler, run code before and after await continuation(request, context), and register it with options.Interceptors.Add<LoggingInterceptor>(). It plays the same role middleware plays for HTTP endpoints.

A browser's JavaScript APIs (fetch, XHR) give no access to HTTP/2 frames and trailers, and gRPC depends on both: it sends its status in the trailers after the body and streams messages in frames. Browsers also decide the connection details themselves, so a page cannot demand HTTP/2 end to end. gRPC-Web changes the wire format so it works over what fetch can do (trailers are encoded in the body). The cost is that it supports unary and server streaming, but not client or bidirectional streaming.

A backend-for-frontend (BFF) fits when the browser's needs differ from the internal service API. The BFF is a small REST or GraphQL service for one front end: it combines several gRPC calls into one response, holds the cookie session and token so tokens never reach the browser, and shapes data for the screen. Transcoding is a mechanical one-to-one translation of each gRPC method to a REST route, so it suits public access to the same API. If the page needs aggregation, a BFF is better; if you just need the same methods over JSON, use transcoding.

Yes. gRPC runs over HTTP/2 by default, and .NET supports gRPC over HTTP/3 (QUIC) on Kestrel and in HttpClient where the platform supports it. HTTP/3 removes head-of-line blocking at the transport level, so one lost packet does not stall all streams on the connection, and it recovers well on mobile networks. Today HTTP/2 is by far the common choice, since HTTP/3 needs UDP to be allowed through firewalls and proxies. Check the current version's documentation before relying on it.

code.title: Protobuf field numbers: safe and unsafe changes

followUps: Because proto3 returns the default value (0, empty string, false) when a field is absent, so a stored 0 and a missing field look the same on the wire. If discount = 0 and "no discount info" mean different things, you cannot tell them apart. Fixes: mark the field optional (proto3 supports this again and generates a presence flag, such as HasDiscount), or use wrapper types like google.protobuf.Int32Value, which can be null. Use presence whenever "not provided" has a meaning of its own.

The enum field keeps the number it received, even if the old client has no name for it. In C# it is stored as the underlying integer, so reading it gives a number that does not match any named member, and the client does not fail while parsing. In proto3 enums are open: the first value must be zero and it is the default, so name it UNKNOWN. Clients should handle unknown values safely, for example by showing "unknown status" instead of crashing on a switch with no default branch.

Keep them in one repository that the teams share, not copied in each service. Common choices: a dedicated protos repository referenced as a Git submodule or packaged as a NuGet package that contains the generated C# code; or a single mono-repo. Version them with the same care as an API: breaking changes are rejected in CI with a tool such as buf breaking, which compares the new files with the last released ones and fails on a removed field or a changed type. A single owner or review rule on that repository stops quiet, incompatible edits.

code.title: GraphQL field selection returns only what is asked

followUps: A query reads data and may be run in parallel; a mutation changes data and its top-level fields run one after another; a subscription opens a long-lived connection (usually WebSocket) so the server can push each new event to the client. They look alike in the language but differ in the rules the server applies. Example: query fetches order 5, mutation cancelOrder(id: 5) cancels it, subscription orderStatusChanged(id: 5) sends a message each time its status changes.

GraphQL avoids numbered versions and instead evolves one schema continuously. Add new fields freely, since clients only get fields they ask for. For a field you want to remove, mark it with @deprecated(reason: "Use fullName"), watch from the query logs which clients still use it, and delete it when usage reaches zero. Breaking changes are limited to removing or changing a field, which you avoid by deprecating first. That is the reason GraphQL providers say "versionless", though you still need the discipline and the usage tracking.

Because every GraphQL call is normally a POST to one URL, and caches key on the method and the URL. A CDN cannot tell that two POST bodies ask the same question, and POST is not cached by default. Workarounds: use GET for queries so the URL contains the query; use persisted queries, where the client sends only a hash like ?id=abc123; and cache on the client with a normalised store keyed by type and id. Server-side, cache per field or per resolver (for example with DataLoader and Redis).

code.title: Calling GraphQL over HTTP and checking errors

followUps: A normalised cache stores each object once under a key made from its type and id, such as Order:5, and the query results hold references to these entries. When a mutation returns the updated Order:5, every screen that shows that order updates at once, with no refetch, because they all read the same entry. Apollo Client and Relay do this. The price is that every object needs a stable id (id and __typename), and you need to handle list changes by hand, because the cache cannot know a new order belongs in a list.

GraphQL can return data and errors together with HTTP 200, for example when 1 field out of 20 fails and becomes null while the rest is fine. Check the errors array every time, not only the HTTP status. Decide per screen: show what you have and mark the failed part, or treat any error as failure. Each error has a path, such as ["orders", 3, "customer"], so you can tell which part failed. Clients such as Apollo expose errorPolicy (none, ignore, all) to choose this behaviour.

A persisted query replaces the full query text with a short id the server already knows. The build step extracts all queries from the front end and registers them with the server. At run time the client sends {"id":"abc123","variables":{...}}. Benefits: smaller requests, GET support (so CDNs can cache), and security, because the server can refuse any query that is not on the list, so attackers cannot send an expensive custom one. Apollo also has automatic persisted queries, which register hashes on first use.

Because mutations change data, and the order of changes can matter. If one request has mutation { a: reserveStock(...) b: chargeCard(...) }, running them in parallel could charge before stock is reserved. The GraphQL specification therefore requires top-level mutation fields to run serially, in the order written. Queries have no side effects, so their fields can run in parallel. Fields nested inside a mutation's result are still resolved in parallel as usual. If you want independent operations to run in parallel, send them as separate requests.

Use a subscription when the client needs changes as soon as they happen and polling would be wasteful or slow: a live order status, chat messages, a dashboard of prices. Polling a query every 5 seconds from 10,000 clients is 2,000 requests a second, mostly returning "nothing new". The cost of subscriptions is that each client holds an open connection, which needs memory, a scale-out plan (a backplane such as Redis) and reconnect logic. For something changing a few times an hour, polling or a webhook is simpler.

Return expected failures as data in the mutation result, and keep the top-level errors array for unexpected ones. A common design is a union or payload type: createOrder(...) { order { id } userErrors { field message } }, so the client gets userErrors: [{field: "quantity", message: "Must be at least 1"}] with HTTP 200. The schema documents these cases, the client can switch on them, and form fields can show each message. Use the errors array, with a code in extensions, for things like unauthenticated or server faults.

code.title: N+1 queries fixed with a DataLoader

followUps: Because a cache that lived longer would show one user's data to another and would go stale. A DataLoader caches by key, such as customer id 10. If it were shared between requests, user A's request could receive a cached customer record that was loaded under user B's permissions, or a value that was changed a minute ago. Creating a new DataLoader for each request keeps the cache valid only for that one query, where the data is consistent and the user is the same. In ASP.NET Core with HotChocolate, register it as a scoped service.

Yes. Any API that returns a list and then calls back for each row has it. A REST client that fetches /orders and then /customers/{id} for each of 20 orders makes 21 calls, and a controller that loops over orders and queries the database for each one also does. Fixes in REST: include related data (?expand=customer), provide a batch endpoint (/customers?ids=10,20,30), or in EF Core use Include or a projection with Select, which makes one SQL query with a join. GraphQL makes the problem easier to hit because resolvers run per field.

When the data is in the same database and you control the query, a projection is simpler and faster: db.Orders.Select(o => new { o.Id, CustomerName = o.Customer.Name }) becomes a single SQL join. A DataLoader still needs a second query and a lookup in memory. Use a DataLoader when the child data comes from another service or database, or when the resolver tree is deep and dynamic, so you cannot know in advance which joins are needed. In short: join if you can, batch if you cannot.

code.title: Query depth and cost limits

followUps: You give every field a price and add them up before running the query. A common rule: each field costs 1, and a list field multiplies the cost of its children by the page size you requested (first: 100), as the program above shows. A query asking for 100 orders, each with 100 items, costs about 10,000 and is refused when the limit is 1,000. Calculate it from the parsed query, not from running it, so a hostile query costs almost nothing. Always require a page size argument, with a maximum, on every list field.

Because a single endpoint serves every query, and a query can reach data through different paths. If you only check "may this user call /graphql", then order { customer { email } } might expose emails to someone who may see orders but not personal data. The same object can be reached from orders, customer.orders and search, so a check in one resolver misses the others. Put the check on the field or the type (an attribute or policy on email, or a data filter at the repository), so every path to the data goes through it.

Introspection lets a client ask the server for its whole schema, which tools like GraphiQL and code generators need. Disabling it in production hides your schema from attackers browsing for hidden fields. The downside is that it is only obscurity: a determined attacker can guess names from error messages (field suggestions) or from your own front-end bundle, so it does not replace authorization. It also breaks tooling for legitimate partners. A balanced choice: leave it on for authenticated developers and in test, turn it off for anonymous production traffic, and turn off field suggestions.

The browser EventSource API has no way to set request headers, so you cannot add Authorization: Bearer .... Options: use a cookie (the browser sends it automatically, with same-site rules in mind); pass a short-lived one-time ticket in the query string, which the server exchanges for the user and which expires in seconds (never the long-lived access token in a URL, as URLs are logged); or skip EventSource and read the stream yourself with fetch and a stream reader, or a library, which does allow headers.

With a normal HTTP request that asks to upgrade. The client sends a GET with Connection: Upgrade, Upgrade: websocket and a random Sec-WebSocket-Key. If the server agrees it answers 101 Switching Protocols with Sec-WebSocket-Accept, a hash of that key. After that the same TCP connection stops speaking HTTP and carries WebSocket frames in both directions. Because the start is plain HTTP, cookies and the Origin header are sent, which the server should check to prevent other sites from opening connections for a logged-in user.

SignalR is the layer on top that you would otherwise write yourself: automatic fallback to server-sent events or long polling when WebSockets are blocked, automatic reconnect, a hub model where clients call server methods and the server calls client methods by name, groups and user targeting (Clients.Group("room1")), JSON or MessagePack serialisation, authentication integration, and scale-out through a Redis or Azure SignalR backplane. A raw WebSocket gives you only a stream of messages, and you must design all of the above.

A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is a side queue where the broker puts messages it could not process: those that failed too many times, expired, or were rejected. Without it, one bad message would be retried forever and block the queue. In Azure Service Bus every queue and subscription has one built in, and a message goes there after MaxDeliveryCount (default 10). The owning team looks at it: an alert on DLQ depth, a dashboard, and a tool to inspect, fix and resubmit messages. A DLQ nobody watches is a silent data-loss bug.

Use ordered delivery per key, not for the whole queue. In Service Bus enable sessions and set the SessionId to the order id: all messages of one session are delivered in order to one consumer at a time, while different orders are processed in parallel. In Kafka the same idea is the partition key: messages with the same key go to the same partition, and a partition is ordered. A single global order would limit you to one consumer, which does not scale. Also design handlers to cope with duplicates, since ordering does not remove them.

The outbox pattern solves "save to the database and publish a message" without a distributed transaction. In one local transaction you write the business change and a row in an Outbox table. A separate process reads unsent rows, publishes them to the broker, and marks them sent. If it crashes between publish and mark, the row is sent again, so consumers must be idempotent (at-least-once delivery). Without it, a crash between SaveChanges and Publish leaves a saved order that nobody hears about.

Head-of-line blocking is when one slow or lost item at the front of a queue stops everything behind it. In HTTP/1.1 a connection handles one request at a time, so a slow response blocks the next ones on it (browsers open several connections to cope). HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams on one TCP connection, which fixes this at the HTTP level, but one lost TCP packet still stalls all streams. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, where each stream recovers on its own, so loss affects only the stream it hit.

Clients can ask for expensive things. A request such as $expand=Customer($expand=Orders($expand=Items)) with $filter on an unindexed column can force huge joins, and $top=1000000 returns the whole table. Controls: cap $top and the number of $expand levels, allow filtering and ordering only on indexed properties, set a maximum query cost, apply authorization before the query is built, and prefer projecting to DTOs over exposing entities. OData is powerful, so limits are part of the design, not an extra.

At the edge, for most systems: a gateway, load balancer or front door (Azure Front Door, Application Gateway) terminates TLS, holds the certificate, and forwards plain HTTP or re-encrypted traffic to the services. That centralises certificates and lets the edge inspect traffic (WAF). For sensitive data, or if compliance asks for encryption in transit everywhere, re-encrypt to the backend (TLS to the pod), or use mutual TLS from a service mesh. Say which choice you made and why, since "TLS ends at the load balancer" means internal traffic is readable on the network.

code.title: Webhook signature, replay window and duplicates

followUps: Because a normal string comparison stops at the first character that differs, so the time it takes leaks how many leading characters were right. An attacker who can measure response times can guess a signature one character at a time. A constant-time comparison always looks at every byte and takes the same time whether it matches or not. In .NET use CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals(a, b) on the two byte arrays; the program above does it by hand for illustration. Over a network the difference is tiny, but the fix is free, so always use it.

The signature is computed from the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If you parse the JSON and serialise it again, whitespace, key order, number format or Unicode escaping can change, and the signature no longer matches even though the data is the same. So read the raw request body first (in ASP.NET Core call Request.EnableBuffering() and read the stream, or read it into a string or byte array before model binding), compute the HMAC over it, and only then parse. Parsing first is a common cause of "signature mismatch" in production.

Support two secrets at the same time for a short overlap. Steps: 1) create the new secret and store it next to the old one; 2) the receiver accepts a signature made with either secret; 3) tell the sender to start signing with the new one (or switch it on your side if you are the sender); 4) after the overlap, for example 24 hours or when no old signatures arrive, remove the old secret. Give each secret an id (a key id in a header) so the receiver knows which to use. No events are dropped, and the change can be undone while both are valid.

The load balancer may send the first request of a connection (negotiate) to server A and the next one to server B. SignalR's handshake and long-polling or SSE fallback need all requests of one connection to hit the same server, because that server holds the connection state. The backplane (Redis, Azure SignalR Service) only passes messages between servers, so a broadcast on A reaches clients on B; it does not move a connection. If only WebSockets are allowed and you skip negotiation (SkipNegotiation = true), no sticky sessions are needed. Otherwise turn on cookie or IP affinity.

Pass the token when the connection starts, because browsers cannot set headers on WebSockets. The client uses accessTokenFactory, and SignalR sends the token as the access_token query string value for WebSockets and SSE. On the server, configure JwtBearerEvents.OnMessageReceived to read the token from the query string when the path starts with /hubs. Then [Authorize] on the hub works, and Context.UserIdentifier is the user id. Keep the access token short-lived, and note that the URL may show up in logs, so mask the query string there.

Send to the user, not to a connection: Clients.User(userId).SendAsync("OrderUpdated", dto). SignalR keeps a list of connection ids per user id (taken from the NameIdentifier claim, or from an IUserIdProvider you supply), and the message goes to all of them, so all 3 tabs receive it. Use Clients.Caller only for the connection that made the call, Clients.Group(name) for a room, and Clients.Client(connectionId) for one connection. With a backplane this works across servers too.

A unit test runs one class (or a small group of them) on its own, with its dependencies replaced by fakes, so it needs no database, network or web server and runs in milliseconds. An integration test runs several real parts together, for example the real controller, routing, validation and a real or containerised database, to prove they work together. Unit tests find logic errors fast and point at the exact place; integration tests find wiring problems, such as a missing DI registration, wrong JSON names or a SQL error. You need both, in a ratio like 70 / 25 / 5 with end-to-end tests.

I do not use a number as a goal, because a team can reach 90% with tests that assert nothing. I use coverage to find untested areas and set a floor, such as 70 to 80% on new code, checked in the pull request, with the stricter target on business logic and none on generated code. What matters more: do the tests fail when behaviour breaks? A useful check is mutation testing (Stryker.NET) on important code, which changes the code and sees whether a test fails. Also review the tests for the risky paths: money, permissions and data loss.

Fast tests on every commit and pull request: unit tests plus a small set of integration tests (in-memory host, containerised database), finishing in under 10 minutes. Slower tests run before a release or overnight: the full integration set, contract tests against other services, UI end-to-end tests, load tests and security scans. The rule is feedback speed: the longer a test takes, the later it runs. A short smoke test (3 to 5 calls) also runs after each deployment to confirm it is alive.

Capture the value from the first response and put it in a variable. In Postman, a test script on the first request runs pm.collectionVariables.set("orderId", pm.response.json().id), and the second request uses {{orderId}} in its URL. In a .http file you name the request with # @name createOrder and use {{createOrder.response.body.$.id}} later. In curl you use id=$(curl ... | jq -r .id) in a shell script. The idea is the same everywhere: extract, store, reuse.

Collections are good for exploring and for simple smoke checks, but they are weak as a main test suite. The tests are JavaScript snippets inside a GUI, hard to review in a pull request and hard to reuse; there is no compile-time safety or refactoring support; test data setup and clean-up are awkward; and the logic cannot be shared with the application. Code-based tests (xUnit with WebApplicationFactory) run in the same build, debug in the IDE, and use the real types. Run Postman collections through Newman only as an external smoke test.

Use the same flow the real client uses, with a test identity. For Microsoft Entra ID, request a token with the client-credentials flow for an app registration made for testing (curl -d "grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=...&client_secret=...&scope=api://<app>/.default" to the tenant's token endpoint), or use az account get-access-token --resource ... for your own user. Postman can fetch a token itself under the Authorization tab. Never paste a token into a shared file, never use production secrets for testing, and keep the secret in an environment variable or a vault.

code.title: Unit test with hand-written fakes

followUps: They differ in what they do. A stub returns fixed answers so the test can run ("Exists(5) returns true"). A mock records how it was used and the test checks that ("Send was called once with this address"). A fake is a working but simple version, such as an in-memory repository built on a dictionary. A dummy only fills a parameter. Prefer checking the result or state (stub or fake) over checking calls (mock), because tests that verify calls break whenever you refactor the inside, even if the behaviour stays the same.

When the test repeats the implementation. If a test needs 8 mock setups and verifies every call in order, it only proves that the code calls what it calls; any refactor breaks it, and it can pass while the real system fails because the mocks were wrong. Signs: more mock code than test logic, tests that change with every code change, and bugs that unit tests missed but integration tests caught. The cure is to mock only at the edges (repository, HTTP, clock), use fakes for the inside, and cover the wiring with integration tests.

Not much for most teams. Both do the same job: Moq has Setup and Verify, NSubstitute has a shorter syntax (repo.Exists(5).Returns(true), email.Received(1).Send(...)). Choose one for the whole solution and keep to it. One caution is that Moq's maintainers added a data-collecting package in 2023, which made some companies move away, so check your organisation's policy. What matters far more is how you design the test: a clear name, one behaviour, and no over-specified expectations.

Reset the state before every test, or isolate each test. Options, from simplest: run each test inside a transaction that is rolled back; use a fresh database per test class (a container, or a unique name); use a library such as Respawn to delete all rows between tests quickly; or have every test create its own data with unique values (a new GUID as a customer id) and never depend on rows left by others. With the EF Core in-memory provider each test class needs a unique database name. Avoid a shared database that tests modify without cleaning.

Because the unit test calls the controller method directly and sees only the returned CreatedAtActionResult, which holds the values you built. The real Location header is produced later by the framework from the route table and the URL helper, and a wrong route name or a missing route parameter only fails then. An integration test sends a real HTTP request through routing and reads response.Headers.Location, so it catches this. The same applies to JSON naming, content types, status codes from filters, and authentication, which a direct method call skips.

Keep the number of tests that touch the database small and make them cheap. Share one host and one container for the whole run (a collection fixture), not one per test; reset data with Respawn, which is faster than recreating the schema; run test classes in parallel with separate databases when the machine allows; and use an in-memory or SQLite database only for logic that does not depend on SQL Server behaviour. Cache the NuGet packages and Docker images in the build. Put slower end-to-end tests in a separate nightly job. The target is a pull request check under 10 minutes.

Treat the queue message as the input and the function as a thin wrapper. Move the real logic into a service class (IBookingProcessor.Process(message)) and unit test that with plain objects. For the function itself, create it with a fake service and a test ILogger (NullLogger), build the message object by hand (the trigger type is just a class or a string), call the method, and check what the fake received. You do not need the Functions runtime for this. Test the binding configuration (queue name, connection setting) with an integration test against Azurite, the local storage emulator.

In the isolated worker model the function is a normal .NET program that you control: it has its own Program.cs, uses standard dependency injection, and gets the FunctionContext and bindings as plain parameters. Your function classes are therefore ordinary classes with constructor injection, which are easy to unit test. In the older in-process model the function ran inside the host's process with its own assembly versions and some types (IAsyncCollector) tied to the host. In-process support ends in November 2026, so new work should use isolated.

Separate the schedule from the work. The timer trigger method should only call a service (await reports.RunDailyAsync(DateTime.UtcNow)), and the test calls that service directly with the time you choose, or passes a fake clock (TimeProvider in .NET 8 and later, with FakeTimeProvider from the testing package). To test the CRON expression itself, use a library that parses it (such as Cronos) and assert the next occurrence from a fixed date. Never wait for the timer, and never test with Thread.Sleep.
