followUps: Let the stub return a failure first and then a success, and count the requests it saw, as the program above does: 503, then 200, expecting exactly 2 requests and a result from the second answer. For backoff delays, give the policy a fake TimeProvider or a delay that you control, so the test does not really wait and can assert "waited 200 ms, then 400 ms". Also test the negative cases: it does not retry a 400, and it stops after the maximum number of tries. In the standard resilience handler these are settings, so your test mainly checks that they are applied to the client you registered.

Yes, stubs drift: the real API changes and your stub keeps answering the old way, so the tests pass while production fails. Reduce the risk by building stubs from the real contract (generate from its OpenAPI file or record real responses), by running contract tests or a small set of tests against the provider's sandbox in a scheduled job, and by sharing the contract with the provider (consumer-driven contracts). Keep stub data realistic, including the odd cases such as empty lists, nulls, long strings and error shapes.

Make the handler wait longer than the client's timeout, or throw the exception the client would throw. A stub handler can do await Task.Delay(Timeout.Infinite, token) and the client's own timeout (HttpClient.Timeout or a resilience timeout) cancels it, which gives a TaskCanceledException. Set the timeout to 100 ms in the test so it is quick. Alternatively throw new HttpRequestException(...) or return a 504 directly. Then assert what your code does: retries, returns a fallback value, or reports the error.

code.title: Detect breaking changes between two schemas

followUps: Both sides share it, but one team must own the process. In consumer-driven contracts the consumer writes the expectations (the fields it really uses), and the provider must keep them passing; the provider owns the code, while consumers own what they require. Put the contracts in a broker such as PactFlow, so the provider's pipeline fetches the latest from every consumer and runs against them. A provider team that breaks a contract sees which consumer and which field in its own build. For a schema (OpenAPI) approach, the provider owns the schema and consumers review changes.

A contract test checks one boundary in isolation: "when I call the provider like this, I get a response of this shape", using a stub on one side and the contract on the other. It is fast and runs on every build. An end-to-end test runs the real system with real deployments of every service and checks a whole journey, such as placing an order. End-to-end tests give high confidence but are slow, flaky and hard to debug; contract tests catch interface breaks earlier and cheaper. Use many contract tests and few end-to-end tests.

Treat it as a planned, versioned change, not as a failure. The usual steps: add the new behaviour next to the old one (a new field or version) so both contracts pass; ask consumers to move and to update their contracts; check in the broker, with its "can I deploy" check, that no consumer still depends on the old behaviour; then remove it. The pipeline blocks a premature removal. If you must break it, publish the new version of the API and run both until the last consumer has moved.

code.title: Percentiles versus average response time

followUps: The average hides the slow requests that users actually notice. In the program above, 18 requests took around 100 ms and 2 took 2 seconds, giving an average of 310 ms: no real request took that long, and the 2-second users are invisible. Averages also move little when a few requests are very slow. Percentiles show the experience of a group: p50 is the typical request, p95 and p99 are the slow tail. Set service goals on percentiles ("p95 under 500 ms") and look at the full histogram, not one number.

A stress test raises the load until the system breaks, to find the limit and see how it fails and recovers: at what request rate do errors start, and does it come back by itself? A soak test (endurance test) holds a normal load for hours to find slow problems such as memory leaks, growing connection counts, full disks or token expiry. There is also a spike test, a sudden jump in load, and a load test, which checks expected peak traffic. Each answers a different question, so say which you are running.

A slow tail with a healthy median means most requests are fine and a few take a different, slower path. Look for: a cold cache or first-request cost; a query that is slow only for certain data (a large customer, a missing index on a rare filter); lock waits or contention; garbage collection pauses; retries and timeouts to a dependency (a 1-second timeout and a retry shows up as 2 seconds); thread-pool starvation; and a connection being reopened. Group traces by the slow requests and compare them with the fast ones (Application Insights, OpenTelemetry) to find the differing step.

Set a fallback authorization policy that requires an authenticated user on every endpoint (options.FallbackPolicy = new AuthorizationPolicyBuilder().RequireAuthenticatedUser().Build()), so a forgotten attribute means "login required", and public endpoints must say [AllowAnonymous] on purpose. Add a code review rule for new endpoints.

Because 403 confirms that the order exists, which tells an attacker which ids are valid and lets them count customers or find numbers worth probing. Returning 404 for "not yours" gives the same answer as "never existed". The trade-off is that a genuine user who mistyped gets less help, and support has more to debug, so log the real reason on the server (with the user id and resource id) but return 404 to the caller. Use 403 when the caller already knows the resource exists, such as a shared document they were told about.

Don't wait: take control of the clock or the token. In a unit test of your validation code, use a fake TimeProvider and advance it past the expiry. In an integration test with a test authentication handler, create tokens yourself with a short lifetime, an exp claim in the past, and ClockSkew = TimeSpan.Zero set in TokenValidationParameters, then assert a 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token". Also test a token that is not valid yet (nbf in the future) and one just inside the lifetime.

code.title: Fake clock instead of Thread.Sleep

followUps: Measure instead of guessing. Make the CI system record the result of every test run (the test results file) and look for tests that both passed and failed on the same commit, or that pass on a retry. Many tools report a flakiness rate per test: Azure DevOps has flaky test management, and you can build a simple query on stored results. Rerun a suspected test 50 or 100 times in a loop (dotnet test --filter ... in a loop) to reproduce it. Quarantine confirmed flaky tests into a separate job, give each an owner and a date, and fix or delete them; do not leave them ignored.

Give each test worker its own database or schema, because parallel tests that write to one database interfere with each other. Options: a template database that is cloned per worker, a container per test class, or a unique schema name (test_ab12) created from migrations. If you use one shared database, tests must use unique data (a new GUID per test) and never assert on counts of all rows. Keep the setup cost low by creating the databases once per run, and put the tests that cannot be isolated into a serial group.

Thread.Sleep(2000) is a guess: if the machine is slow it is too short and the test fails randomly; if it is fast you wasted 2 seconds. Add 500 such tests and a build takes extra 17 minutes. Replace it by waiting for the condition: poll with a short interval and a timeout (await Eventually(() => queue.IsEmpty, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5))), await the task or a TaskCompletionSource that the code completes, or replace the clock with a fake one so time moves only when the test says.

I block a merge for anything that can lose or leak data, break existing clients, or fail under load: a missing owner check, a changed response shape without a version, a write endpoint without idempotency or concurrency control, unbounded lists with no paging, secrets in code, and no tests for the new behaviour. I leave as comments, not blockers: naming, small style differences, extra ideas, and refactors that are not part of the change. Marking each comment as "must fix" or "suggestion" makes the difference clear and keeps the review from stalling on opinions.

I would first ask for it to be split, because reviewers miss problems in large changes. If that is not possible, I review in layers: start with the description and the tests to understand the intent; read the contract changes (routes, DTOs, migrations) closely; then the risky logic (authorization, money, data access); and skim generated code and renames. I review in several short sessions, not one long one, and sometimes pair with the author on a call. I agree a size rule with the team, for example under 400 changed lines, with large changes needing a design note first.

Turn the list into something automatic and shared. Put it in the pull request template as a short checklist; write analyzers and architecture tests for what can be checked by machine (every endpoint has authorization, no entity returned from a controller); add the API-diff and contract checks to CI; and write one or two "good example" endpoints the team can copy. Review with the team in the first few weeks and explain the reason for each rule, so people learn the thinking. The goal is that the checks catch it first, and my review is about design, not the list.

It breaks things you did not expect. Browsers prefetch links, search engines crawl them, email scanners open every URL in a message, and proxies retry GETs, so a GET that deletes an order will delete orders when someone merely previews a link or a crawler visits. A cache may also answer the GET itself, so the delete never reaches the server. Another site can trigger it with a hidden image tag in the victim's logged-in browser. That is why GET must be safe: only read.

PUT /api/v1/users/42/avatar or PUT /api/v1/files/report-2026.pdf: the client chooses the URL, and the first call creates the resource and returns 201, while later calls replace it and return 200 or 204. Another example is a document stored under a name or a settings entry with a known key: PUT /users/42/settings/theme with {"value":"dark"}. It stays idempotent, since repeating it leaves the same result.

Rarely in a real project, and that is an honest answer. I use the parts that are cheap and useful: the Location header after a 201 or 202, next links in paged responses, and a status link for a long-running job. I have not built clients that discover every action by following links, because the front end team knows the routes already and the extra effort in response size, tooling and testing rarely pays. If the allowed actions depend on state (cancel, refund), a list of links such as "actions": ["cancel"] is a practical middle path.

A SAS (shared access signature) token is a URL with a signature that grants limited access to an Azure Storage resource without sharing the account key. It says which blob or container, which permissions (read, write), from when to when, and optionally which IP, and it is signed with a key. Keep it as short as the task allows: minutes for a single upload or download, not days. Prefer a user delegation SAS (signed with an Entra ID identity) over an account-key SAS, because it can be revoked by removing the identity, and store the lifetime in code so nobody invents a one-year token.

Use RPC style when the action is not a simple change to a resource, or when it is a command with rules and side effects. Examples: POST /orders/5/cancel, POST /payments/refund, POST /reports/generate. Forcing these into PUT or PATCH on a "status" field hides the business operation and the rules around it. It is also the natural fit for gRPC between internal services. A pragmatic API mixes the two: resources for CRUD, named action endpoints for real commands, each with a clear name and a documented result.

Use a resumable upload. The client starts a session (POST /uploads returns an upload id and URL), sends the file in chunks (for example 4 MB), and the server records how many bytes it has. After a failure the client asks HEAD /uploads/{id} (or GET status) for the stored offset, and continues from byte 80,000,000 instead of 0. Standards and products that do this: the tus protocol, Azure Blob Storage block upload (PutBlock then PutBlockList), and S3 multipart upload. Expire unfinished sessions after a day.

A managed identity is an identity in Entra ID that Azure creates and manages for a resource, such as an App Service or Function. The app asks Azure for a token for the target service (Key Vault, Storage, SQL) and Azure checks which identity is asking. There is no secret to store, nothing to leak in config or source control, nothing to rotate or to expire at 2 a.m. A client secret is a password: it must be stored, rotated and kept out of logs. In .NET use DefaultAzureCredential, which uses the managed identity in Azure and your developer sign-in locally.

Anything that is business logic. A gateway (such as Azure API Management or YARP) should handle cross-cutting, uniform concerns: TLS, authentication of the token, rate limits, routing, caching, request size limits and logging. It should not hold rules like "gold customers get a discount", reshape data in complex ways, or call several services to build a response, since it becomes a hidden second application that is hard to test and version. Keep rules in services. If you need aggregation for a screen, use a backend-for-frontend service you can test in code.

Support two keys at once for an overlap period. Issue the new key to the client while the old one still works; the server accepts either (store only hashes of keys, with an id and an expiry date for each); the client switches when ready; and when usage of the old key reaches zero, or after the agreed date, you revoke it. Offer the client a way to create a second key themselves. Log which key id each call used so you know who is still on the old one. Design for rotation from day one, since emergency rotation after a leak is much harder.
